title: Over-the-counter medicines: adult label directions
summary: Adult label doses, intervals, daily limits and key warnings for seven common OTC medicines, taken straight from their drug labels.

sources.title: DailyMed - Tylenol Extra Strength (acetaminophen 500 mg) label
DailyMed - Naproxen sodium 220 mg (Kirkland Signature) label
American Diabetes Association - Diabetes and Planning for Sick Days

blocks.text: This table is for **adults and children 12 and over** and follows one example label for each medicine. Your package may have a different strength or wording, so **your package wins**. For anyone under 12, follow the dosing on the package by weight or age, or ask a doctor. If someone takes too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (printed on the acetaminophen label) or get medical help right away, even with no symptoms.

rows: 6 caplets, unless a doctor says otherwise

Severe liver damage can happen with more than 4,000 mg in 24 hours, with any other acetaminophen product, or with 3 or more alcoholic drinks a day. Ask a doctor first with liver disease; ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take warfarin. Do not use more than 10 days for pain or 3 days for fever without a doctor. Rare severe skin reactions: stop and get help.
1 tablet. If pain or fever does not respond, 2 tablets.
Every 4 to 6 hours while symptoms last
6 tablets, unless a doctor says otherwise

NSAID. Raises risk of heart attack, heart failure, stroke and severe stomach bleeding (higher at 60 or older, with ulcers, blood thinners, steroids, other NSAIDs, or 3 or more drinks a day). Ask a doctor first with high blood pressure, heart disease, liver cirrhosis, kidney disease, asthma, or if you take a diuretic. Not at 20 weeks of pregnancy or later unless a doctor directs. Stop and ask a doctor if pain lasts more than 10 days or fever more than 3 days.
1 tablet. For the first dose you may take 2 within the first hour.
Every 8 to 12 hours while symptoms last
3 tablets; no more than 2 in any 8 to 12 hours

NSAID, so the same heart, stroke, stomach-bleeding, kidney, asthma and pregnancy warnings as ibuprofen. Drink a full glass of water with each dose. Stop and ask a doctor if pain lasts more than 10 days or fever more than 3 days.

Marked drowsiness: avoid alcohol, use care driving. Do not use with any other diphenhydramine product, even on the skin. Ask a doctor first with emphysema, chronic bronchitis, glaucoma, or trouble urinating from an enlarged prostate. Ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take sedatives or tranquilizers.
2 softgels after the first loose stool, then 1 after each loose stool

More than directed can cause serious heart problems or death. Do not use with bloody or black stool. Ask a doctor first with fever, mucus in the stool, liver disease or abnormal heart rhythm. Drink plenty of clear fluids. Stop and ask a doctor if it gets worse, lasts more than 2 days, or the belly swells.
Ask a doctor first with liver or kidney disease.

May cause drowsiness; avoid alcohol; use care driving. Ask a doctor first with liver or kidney disease. Ask a doctor or pharmacist if you take sedatives or tranquilizers. Age 65 and over: ask a doctor. Do not use if allergic to hydroxyzine.

blocks.text: Things to know if you have type 1 diabetes

items: Ask your diabetes team which cold and flu medicines are safe. ADA says some can raise blood sugar or interact with your usual medicines.

Dexcom G7: acetaminophen up to 1 gram every 6 hours is fine for treatment decisions, but more than that in an adult may make sensor readings look higher than they are. Other CGMs differ, so read your own guide.
Ibuprofen and naproxen labels list kidney disease among the conditions to ask a doctor about first.
Vomiting or diarrhea in type 1 diabetes can lead to dehydration and DKA. Follow the sick-day guide, not just the anti-diarrhea label.
For a severe allergic reaction, use epinephrine and call 911. See the allergic reaction guide.
